input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-251: Concepts of Parallel and Distributed Systems. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course is an introduction to the organization and programming of systems comprising multiple computers. Topics include the organization of multi-core computers, parallel computer clusters, computing grids, client-server systems, and peer-to-peer systems; computer networks and network protocols; network security; multi-threaded programming; and network programming. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-243 or SWEN-262 or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[nist-cryptographic-standards]
Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block. Validation checks implementations against specified requirements. Security depends on the complete protocol and implementation, not only an algorithm name. Analysis also considers side channels and migration requirements.

[nist-ssdf]
The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development. Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts. Produce Well-Secured Software addresses security requirements, design, verification, and release. Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies, analyzes, remediates, and learns from discovered weaknesses. Security requirements should be tracked throughout development. Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities.

[rit-csci-251]
This course is an introduction to the organization and programming of systems comprising multiple computers. Topics include the organization of multi-core computers, parallel computer clusters, computing grids, client-server systems, and peer-to-peer systems; computer networks and network protocols; network security; multi-threaded programming; and network programming. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-243 or SWEN-262 or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

beats.claim: Parallel and distributed systems organize multiple computers to solve complex problems by sharing resources and coordinating tasks across nodes.
beats.example: A web server cluster distributes incoming HTTP requests across multiple physical machines to handle high traffic loads.
beats.title: Foundations of Parallel and Distributed Architecture
beats.visualDirection: Display a diagram showing a single server versus a cluster of three servers connected by a network, highlighting load distribution.

beats.claim: Multi-core computers contain multiple processing units on a single chip that execute threads concurrently to improve computational throughput.
beats.example: A modern desktop processor with eight cores can execute eight separate program threads simultaneously, reducing execution time for parallelizable workloads.
beats.title: Multi-Core Computer Organization
beats.visualDirection: Show a close-up illustration of a CPU die with eight distinct cores, each labeled with a thread ID, connected via an internal interconnect.

beats.claim: Clusters consist of tightly coupled machines working together, while computing grids aggregate geographically dispersed resources to perform large-scale distributed computations.
beats.example: A scientific research cluster runs molecular dynamics simulations in parallel, whereas a computing grid coordinates thousands of university servers to analyze climate data.
beats.title: Parallel Computer Clusters and Computing Grids
beats.visualDirection: Draw two side-by-side network maps: one showing a local cluster with direct links, and another showing a grid with regional nodes connected via the internet.

beats.claim: Client-server systems centralize resources on dedicated servers accessed by requesting clients, while peer-to-peer systems allow equal participants to share data and services.
beats.example: A bank's online portal uses a client-server model where users connect to central authentication servers, whereas a file-sharing network uses peer-to-peer nodes to exchange documents directly.
beats.title: Client-Server and Peer-to-Peer Systems
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a star topology for client-server with a central server node, and a mesh topology for peer-to-peer with interconnected user nodes.

beats.claim: Computer networks rely on standardized protocols to ensure reliable data transmission, error detection, and resource allocation across distributed nodes.
beats.example: The TCP/IP protocol suite manages packet routing, congestion control, and end-to-end delivery, ensuring that data reaches the correct destination despite network failures.
beats.title: Computer Networks and Network Protocols
beats.visualDirection: Show a packet traversing a network with labeled protocol layers (application, transport, network, link) and a status indicator for successful delivery.

beats.claim: Network security mechanisms protect distributed systems by encrypting data in transit, verifying identities, and preventing unauthorized access to network resources.
beats.example: TLS encryption secures web traffic by encrypting payloads and using digital certificates to authenticate the server, preventing man-in-the-middle attacks.
beats.title: Network Security and Data Protection
beats.visualDirection: Display a flowchart showing plaintext data entering a TLS handshake, being encrypted with a symmetric key, and exiting as ciphertext with an integrity tag.

beats.claim: Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters that ensure confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity when keys and modes are used correctly.
beats.example: AES-256 encryption with a properly rotated key protects sensitive database records, while a nonce ensures each encryption operation produces a unique ciphertext.
beats.title: Cryptographic Standards and Key Management
beats.visualDirection: Show a key management lifecycle diagram with stages: generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, and destruction, each marked with a checkmark.

beats.claim: Multi-threaded programming allows a single process to execute multiple threads concurrently, sharing memory and resources while requiring synchronization to prevent race conditions
beats.example: A web application uses separate threads for handling database queries, user authentication, and response generation, coordinated by mutex locks to protect shared variables.
beats.title: Multi-Threaded Programming Fundamentals
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a process with three threads, each with a stack and shared heap, highlighting a mutex lock protecting a critical section.

beats.claim: Network programming enables distributed systems to exchange messages using sockets, message queues, or RPC frameworks, requiring careful handling of latency and partial failures.
beats.example: A distributed caching system uses UDP multicast to broadcast cache invalidation messages, while a RPC framework serializes requests and deserializes responses across network boundaries.
beats.title: Network Programming and Distributed Communication
beats.visualDirection: Show a sequence diagram of an RPC call: client sends request, server processes, server sends response, client receives result, with timeout indicators.

beats.claim: Secure software development practices group activities into preparation, protection, production, and response phases, ensuring security requirements are tracked and verified.
beats.example: A development team uses a secure software development framework to verify that cryptographic libraries are properly integrated, track security requirements, and remediate vulnerabilities before release.
beats.title: Secure Software Development and Verification
beats.visualDirection: Display a four-box flowchart labeled Prepare, Protect, Produce, Respond, with arrows showing continuous feedback loops and a verification badge.

learningObjectives: Define the core architectural models of parallel and distributed systems, including multi-core, clusters, grids, client-server, and peer-to-peer topol
Explain how network protocols and security mechanisms protect data integrity and confidentiality in distributed environments
Apply multi-threaded and network programming concepts to design and analyze concurrent system components
